title: Qotom Q51551UT 4x 10GbE and 6x 2.5GbE Mini PC Review
gist: ServeTheHome reviews the Qotom Q51551UT, an Intel Core Ultra 5 125H mini-PC with six 2.5GbE (Intel I226-V), two 10GBASE-T (Intel X540-AT2) and two SFP+ 10G (Intel X710-BM2) ports, aimed at firewall, edge and virtualization use. The reviewer notes that every port is at least 2.5GbE, but criticizes the 16-year-old X540 controller that lacks 2.5G/5G NBASE-T speeds and warns that PCIe wiring prevents all NICs from running at full speed at once.

insights.claim: The Qotom Q51551UT mini-PC combines an Intel Core Ultra 5 125H (4P+8E+2LPE), up to 96GB DDR5-5600 as tested, a PCIe Gen5 x8 slot, and 10 Ethernet ports: six 2.5GbE, two 10GBASE-T and two SFP+ 10G.
insights.so_what: Low-cost Chinese mini-PCs now offer multi-10G networking suitable for edge firewalls and home labs.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith

insights.claim: The Qotom Q51551UT has no Ethernet port slower than 2.5GbE, giving it real bandwidth rather than just many connections, which suits software firewalls and edge computing.
insights.so_what: 2.5GbE has become the floor for networking appliances in this class.
insights.quote: Every single port is at least 2.5GbE
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith

insights.claim: Features like five front USB-A ports (only one at 5Gbps), an RJ45 RS-232 serial console port and side-mount-only rubber feet show the Qotom Q51551UT is targeted at the industrial market rather than consumers.
insights.so_what: Positioned as an industrial/edge box, not a consumer desktop.
insights.locator: Starting our brief tour from the front
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith

insights.claim: Qotom's use of Intel's X540-AT2 controller for the 10GBASE-T ports is puzzling because it is a 16-year-old, long-discontinued design that predates NBASE-T, so those ports cannot run at intermediate 2.5Gbps or 5Gbps speeds.
insights.so_what: Buyers with 2.5G/5G switches must plan around these legacy 10G ports.
insights.quote: it is an atypically inflexible design for a modern mini-PC
insights.locator: To the left, we have the first two
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith

insights.claim: The SFP+ ports use Intel's X710-BM2 (Fortville) controller, which is over a decade old but a proven, reliable platform supporting 1GbE or 10GbE modules and easy optical networking, while the six 2.5GbE ports use Intel's modern mainstream I226-V.
insights.so_what: Older Intel NIC silicon still ships in new edge systems because of its reliability.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith

insights.claim: According to Qotom's spec sheet, the Q51551UT cannot run all NICs at full speed at once: each 2.5GbE port has a PCIe Gen2 x1 link and two of the 10G ports share 12Gbps of upstream bandwidth.
insights.so_what: Real aggregate throughput is lower than the port count suggests; check bandwidth for heavy routing workloads.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith

insights.claim: With HDMI 2.0 and DisplayPort 1.4 outputs from the Core Ultra 5's integrated Intel Arc GPU, which supports 4K and Quick Sync, the Qotom Q51551UT can also serve digital signage and run as a Proxmox VE virtualization platform.
insights.so_what: One box covers networking, signage and virtualization, widening its addressable market.
insights.locator: Between those are the system’s display outputs
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith

insights.claim: The Qotom Q51551UT uses active cooling with a low-profile blower, and although its case is labeled 12V it takes a 19V adapter, shipping with a 120W external power supply.
insights.so_what: A minor practical detail for deployments that replace power supplies.
insights.locator: Finally, we can quickly see the DC barrel
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
